name: Archon
description: The first open-source harness builder for AI coding. Make AI coding deterministic and repeatable.
readmeExcerpt:
Archon

The simplest way to build the software that builds your software.
YAML workflows that can do anything.

--- Archon is a factory builder. You describe how work should get done as YAML workflows, and Archon runs them with AI agents, scripts and your decisions in the places that need them. Software is the first factory: the bundled SDLC pack takes an issue to a merged pull request. The same engine runs any process you can describe. Take yourself out of the loop and sit on top of it. Runs do the work, queues keep it moving, and a run comes to you only when it needs a decision you own. ## Why Archon Ask a coding agent to fix a bug and the result depends on the run. It may skip the plan, forget the tests or ignore your PR template. You end up supervising every step. Archon turns your process into a workflow you own. The workflow fixes the steps, the checks and the gates. The agent supplies the judgment inside each step. That gives you: - **The same process every time.** Plan, implement, review, validate, open the PR, in the order you wrote down. - **Human on the loop, not in it.** Queues take work forward on their own. When a run reaches a decision it can't make, it pauses as one attention item: what it is, why it matters, a recommendation and the choices. You answer and it carries on. - **Governance built in.** Approval gates, a full event log and transcript for every run, and the cost of every run, all stored in your own database. - **Your agents, your subscriptions.** Archon is not another coding agent. It runs Claude Code, Codex and Pi through their own CLIs and SDKs, with the accounts and project guidance you already have. - **Self-hosted.** One install on your machine or server. SQLite by default, PostgreSQL if you want it. ## What it looks like A workflow is a graph of nodes. Agents judge, code computes, and you decide where it matters: ```yaml # .archon/workflows/build-feature.yaml name: build-feature description: Plan, implement until the tests pass, ask for approval, open the PR. nodes: - id: plan prompt: "Read the request and the code. Write an implementation plan." - id: implement depends_on: [plan] loop: prompt: "Implement the next step of the plan." until_bash: "bun run test" # your test command; code decides when it is done max_iterations: 10 fresh_context: true - id: approve depends_on: [implement] wait: # the run pauses and asks you attention: "Review the change. Approve, or reject to stop." form: approval - id: stop depends_on: [approve] when: "$approve.output.decision == 'reject'" cancel: "Rejected at review." - id: pr depends_on: [approve] when: "$approve.output.decision == 'approve'" prompt: "Push the branch and open a pull request." ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR plan["plan
(agent)"] --> implement["implement
(agent, loops until the tests pass)"] implement --> approve{"approve
(waits for you)"} approve -- reject --> stop["stop"] approve -- approve --> pr["pr
(agent)"] ``` Save it in your repository's `.archon/workflows/`, swap `bun run test` for your own test command, and run it: ```bash archon workflow run build-feature "Add dark mode to the settings page" ``` Repository runs get their own git worktree by default, so several can work on one repository at once. ## A software factory: issue in, merged PR out The bundled `sdlc` pack is a working factory for a repository: 1. **You open an issue.** `archon-intake` checks it against the current code and decides what it needs: a plan, an investigation, straight to delivery, or a maintainer's look. 2. **The build queue picks it up.** `archon-build-queue` claims the next ready issue, writes the brief and runs `archon-ship`: plan, implement, review through specialist lenses, fix the findings, wait for CI. It stops at a pull request whose review says Ready, asking once for any check no round can run, or at one a maintainer's `ready` answer hands on; the merge gate checks either the same way. 3. **The merge queue lands it.** `archon-merge-queue` merges the clear ready pull requests that merge cleanly, through a gate that checks the review verdict and CI at the head commit and that the base branch is not red. The queue judges open review threads itself and sends a pull request that conflicts back to the build queue. 4. **You answer what's unclear.** A scope question, a schema change or a stuck round becomes one attention item with a recommendation. Your answer is written into the issue as the new scope. 5. **Nothing found along the way is lost.** `archon-discoveries` reads what runs noticed outside their task and files it, tracks it on an existing issue, or drops it. Archon builds Archon: of the 524 pull requests merged into this repository between 1 and 19 October 2026, Archon runs built 363. You start the queues by hand or bind them to a schedule or issue events with a [trigger](https://archon.diy/guides/workflow-triggers/). The pack binds nothing by default. The pack works through the GitHub CLI (`gh`) today; see [the forge path](https://archon.diy/reference/forge/#use-the-forge-path-in-the-sdlc-pack) for the plugin route. [Set up the SDLC factory](https://archon.diy/getting-started/sdlc-factory/) runs it on your repository, and [SDLC pack workflows](https://archon.diy/reference/sdlc-workflows/) describes every workflow in it. ## Build any factory Workflows are not tied to code. A node can be an agent prompt, a bash command, a script, a loop, a wait for a person or a child workflow, so any process with steps, checks and decisions fits: content production, research, operations, support. Write it as YAML, keep its commands and scripts beside it, and share it as a pack. ## A reliable core, extensible at the seams The core stays small: the workflow engine, isolation, durable state, the attention queue and an audit trail. Everything that talks to the outside world plugs in through a published contract, and you can build your own plugin for any of them: | Plugin kind | What it adds | Maintained here | |---|---|---| | Workflow pack | Workflows, commands and scripts | `sdlc` | | Provider | An agent runtime | Claude Code, Codex, Pi | | Forge | A code host | GitHub | | Chat | A conversation surface | Slack | GitHub is the registry: publish in your own repository and install with `archon plugin add owner/repo`. See [Publish a plugin](https://archon.diy/guides/publishing-plugins/) and the [plugin index](https://archon.diy/plugins/). ## Quickstart 1. Install [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code) and sign in, or install Codex. 2. Install Archon. The installer asks which providers to add: ```bash curl -fsSL https://archon.diy/install | bash # macOS / Linux irm https://archon.diy/install.ps1 | iex # Windows (PowerShell) brew install coleam00/archon/archon # Homebrew, then: archon setup ``` 3. Run a workflow in any git repository: ```bash cd your-project archon workflow list archon workflow run archon-investigate "Why does the login test fail?" ``` 4. Watch runs and answer their questions in the web console with `archon serve`, or from the terminal with `archon workflow attention`. To let your coding agent drive Archon for you, run `archon skill add` in your project, then ask it to "use archon to fix issue #42". Other installs (from source, Docker, servers), provider setup and the Claude Code binary path are in the [installation guide](https://archon.diy/getting-started/installation/). The [quick start](https://archon.diy/getting-started/quick-start/) shows how to write a brief a run can deliver against. ## Connect a platform The CLI and web console work out of the box. Archon

The simplest way to build the software that builds your software.
YAML workflows that can do anything.

Archon is a factory builder. You describe how work should get done as YAML workflows, and Archon runs them with AI agents, scripts and your decisions in the places that need them. Software is the first factory: the bundled SDLC pack takes an issue to a merged pull request. The same engine runs any process you can describe.

Take yourself out of the loop and sit on top of it. Runs do the work, queues keep it moving, and a run comes to you only when it needs a decision you own.

Why Archon

Ask a coding agent to fix a bug and the result depends on the run. It may skip the plan, forget the tests or ignore your PR template. You end up supervising every step.

Archon turns your process into a workflow you own. The workflow fixes the steps, the checks and the gates. The agent supplies the judgment inside each step. That gives you:

  • The same process every time. Plan, implement, review, validate, open the PR, in the order you wrote down.
  • Human on the loop, not in it. Queues take work forward on their own. When a run reaches a decision it can't make, it pauses as one attention item: what it is, why it matters, a recommendation and the choices. You answer and it carries on.
  • Governance built in. Approval gates, a full event log and transcript for every run, and the cost of every run, all stored in your own database.
  • Your agents, your subscriptions. Archon is not another coding agent. It runs Claude Code, Codex and Pi through their own CLIs and SDKs, with the accounts and project guidance you already have.
  • Self-hosted. One install on your machine or server. SQLite by default, PostgreSQL if you want it.

What it looks like

A workflow is a graph of nodes. Agents judge, code computes, and you decide where it matters:

# .archon/workflows/build-feature.yaml
name: build-feature
description: Plan, implement until the tests pass, ask for approval, open the PR.
nodes:
  - id: plan
    prompt: "Read the request and the code. Write an implementation plan."

  - id: implement
    depends_on: [plan]
    loop:
      prompt: "Implement the next step of the plan."
      until_bash: "bun run test"          # your test command; code decides when it is done
      max_iterations: 10
      fresh_context: true

  - id: approve
    depends_on: [implement]
    wait:                                 # the run pauses and asks you
      attention: "Review the change. Approve, or reject to stop."
      form: approval

  - id: stop
    depends_on: [approve]
    when: "$approve.output.decision == 'reject'"
    cancel: "Rejected at review."

  - id: pr
    depends_on: [approve]
    when: "$approve.output.decision == 'approve'"
    prompt: "Push the branch and open a pull request."
flowchart LR
  plan["plan<br/>(agent)"] --> implement["implement<br/>(agent, loops until the tests pass)"]
  implement --> approve{"approve<br/>(waits for you)"}
  approve -- reject --> stop["stop"]
  approve -- approve --> pr["pr<br/>(agent)"]
Loading

Save it in your repository's .archon/workflows/, swap bun run test for your own test command, and run it:

archon workflow run build-feature "Add dark mode to the settings page"

Repository runs get their own git worktree by default, so several can work on one repository at once.

A software factory: issue in, merged PR out

The bundled sdlc pack is a working factory for a repository:

  1. You open an issue. archon-intake checks it against the current code and decides what it needs: a plan, an investigation, straight to delivery, or a maintainer's look.
  2. The build queue picks it up. archon-build-queue claims the next ready issue, writes the brief and runs archon-ship: plan, implement, review through specialist lenses, fix the findings, wait for CI. It stops at a pull request whose review says Ready, asking once for any check no round can run, or at one a maintainer's ready answer hands on; the merge gate checks either the same way.
  3. The merge queue lands it. archon-merge-queue merges the clear ready pull requests that merge cleanly, through a gate that checks the review verdict and CI at the head commit and that the base branch is not red. The queue judges open review threads itself and sends a pull request that conflicts back to the build queue.
  4. You answer what's unclear. A scope question, a schema change or a stuck round becomes one attention item with a recommendation. Your answer is written into the issue as the new scope.
  5. Nothing found along the way is lost. archon-discoveries reads what runs noticed outside their task and files it, tracks it on an existing issue, or drops it.

Archon builds Archon: of the 524 pull requests merged into this repository between 1 and 19 October 2026, Archon runs built 363.

You start the queues by hand or bind them to a schedule or issue events with a trigger. The pack binds nothing by default. The pack works through the GitHub CLI (gh) today; see the forge path for the plugin route. Set up the SDLC factory runs it on your repository, and SDLC pack workflows describes every workflow in it.

Build any factory

Workflows are not tied to code. A node can be an agent prompt, a bash command, a script, a loop, a wait for a person or a child workflow, so any process with steps, checks and decisions fits: content production, research, operations, support. Write it as YAML, keep its commands and scripts beside it, and share it as a pack.

A reliable core, extensible at the seams

The core stays small: the workflow engine, isolation, durable state, the attention queue and an audit trail. Everything that talks to the outside world plugs in through a published contract, and you can build your own plugin for any of them:

Plugin kind What it adds Maintained here
Workflow pack Workflows, commands and scripts sdlc
Provider An agent runtime Claude Code, Codex, Pi
Forge A code host GitHub
Chat A conversation surface Slack

GitHub is the registry: publish in your own repository and install with archon plugin add owner/repo. See Publish a plugin and the plugin index.

Quickstart

  1. Install Claude Code and sign in, or install Codex.

  2. Install Archon. The installer asks which providers to add:

    curl -fsSL https://archon.diy/install | bash        # macOS / Linux
irm https://archon.diy/install.ps1 | iex             # Windows (PowerShell)
brew install coleam00/archon/archon                 # Homebrew, then: archon setup

  3. Run a workflow in any git repository:

    cd your-project
archon workflow list
archon workflow run archon-investigate "Why does the login test fail?"

  4. Watch runs and answer their questions in the web console with archon serve, or from the terminal with archon workflow attention.

To let your coding agent drive Archon for you, run archon skill add in your project, then ask it to "use archon to fix issue #42".

Other installs (from source, Docker, servers), provider setup and the Claude Code binary path are in the installation guide. The quick start shows how to write a brief a run can deliver against.

Connect a platform

The CLI and web console work out of the box. Connect a chat platform or forge to start and follow runs from there:

Platform Guide
Slack Slack guide
Telegram Telegram guide
GitHub webhooks GitHub guide
Discord Discord guide

Documentation

Full documentation is at archon.diy/docs.

Topic Description
Quickstart Install and first run
Workflow language Write your own YAML workflows
Operate runs Watch runs, answer the ones that need you, read results
CLI reference Every command and flag
Configuration Config options, model tiers and aliases, env vars
AI assistants Claude Code, Codex and Pi setup
Deployment Docker, VPS and production setup
Architecture Packages and boundaries
Troubleshooting Common issues and fixes

For AI tools: point your LLM at /llms.txt for an index of the docs, /llms-full.txt for all of them in one file, or /llms-small.txt for a condensed version.

Previous version

Looking for the original Python-based Archon (task management and RAG)? It is preserved on the archive/v1-task-management-rag branch.

Telemetry

Archon sends a few anonymous events so maintainers can see which workflows get real usage, on what platforms, and whether runs succeed, and prioritize accordingly. No PII, ever. Events: archon_started (once per CLI invocation or server boot; archon serve reports as the server, and a detached run's worker process is counted by the command that started it), archon_active (daily heartbeat while a server is running, so long-running installs stay counted), chat_turn_handled (each direct AI chat turn: platform, provider, model, duration, and usage totals; never message content), workflow_invoked (each workflow start, and again for each resumed segment), workflow_completed / workflow_failed / workflow_cancelled (sent once when a run's final status is saved, whichever path ended it), workflow_approval_resolved (each human approve/reject decision: the binary resolution only, never comments or reasons), and codebase_registered (a pure count when a project is registered; no name, path, or URL).

What's collected (categorical only):

  • Workflow name: the real name for bundled (Archon-authored) workflows; "custom" for your own workflows, so private names never leave your machine. The discovery source (bundled/global/project) is sent alongside.
  • Run shape & outcome: platform (cli/web/slack/…), provider and model ids, node count, how many nodes of each type, graph depth and widest fan-out, how many distinct commands are referenced, the total inline prompt size as a bucket (none/lt_1k/1k_5k/5k_20k/gte_20k characters), which node types and features are used (loop/approval/script/bash, structured output, persisted sessions, MCP, skills, fresh-context loops), whether the run is interactive, isolated in a worktree, a resume, or a child of another run, the outcome, duration (from the run's first start to its end, including approval and wait time), a categorical exit or cancel reason, and a fixed-enum failure class recorded where the first failed node failed (fatal/transient/unknown for provider errors; timeout, exec_failed, output_contract, max_iterations, child_failed, cancelled, config for engine-detected causes; never raw error text) plus that node's type.
  • Run reference: run_ref, a one-way hash of the install UUID and the run id, so a run's start, resumes and outcome can be joined. The run id itself is never sent.
  • Bundled ancestry: when one of your workflows is a copy of a bundled workflow, the bundled workflow's name and whether the copy is identical or modified (derived_from, derived_similarity). Only the bundled name is sent; nothing about your copy's name, node ids or prompts.
  • Workflow no match: workflow_no_match, a count of agent decisions that no available workflow fits, with only the transport (native_tool or cli).
  • Chat activity: one event per direct-chat AI turn with platform, provider, model, duration, and completed/failed; a turn whose provider errors out mid-turn counts as failed. Message content, prompts, and conversation ids are never sent.
  • Aggregate usage: provider-reported gross input, output, optional cache-read/cache-write token totals (with a flag when those totals are a floor), and cost (USD) per workflow run across all of its resumed segments (a parent run's total includes its child runs' spend, so sum spend over runs that are not children), plus direct-chat usage and total loop iterations. Numeric totals only, never the content the tokens represent.
  • Machine context: OS, architecture, Archon version, runtime, whether it's a binary build, the install channel (binary/docker/source), the short commit of the running build when known, whether stderr is a terminal, and a CI flag.
  • Deployment shape (server only): which adapters are enabled (booleans), how many chat plugins it hosts (a count; plugin names are not sent), database kind (sqlite/postgresql), whether web auth and multi-user mode are on, and the GitHub auth mode. Configuration values (tokens, URLs, hosts) are never sent.
  • A random install UUID stored at $ARCHON_HOME/telemetry-id (~/.archon/telemetry-id by default, /.archon/telemetry-id in Docker). Nothing else.
  • A schema_version number on every event, bumped whenever this list changes.

What's not collected: your code, prompts, messages, custom workflow names, workflow descriptions, git remotes, file paths, usernames, tokens, AI output, error message text, your IP address, your geographic location. None of it.

Opt out: set any of these in your environment:

ARCHON_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1
DO_NOT_TRACK=1        # de facto standard honored by Astro, Bun, Prisma, Nuxt, etc.
POSTHOG_API_KEY=off   # off | 0 | false | disabled | "" all disable

CI environments (CI=true) are auto-disabled: forks running fixtures in GitHub Actions, CircleCI, etc. do not send events.

Check the current state: run archon telemetry status to see whether telemetry is enabled, why (if not), the install UUID, and the active host. Run archon telemetry reset to rotate the install UUID. archon doctor also surfaces the current state in its check list.

Shutdown gives pending telemetry a 75 ms flush window, then cancels outstanding requests. Slow or unreachable ingestion can lose events; it does not hold up command exit. Far from the ingest host (for example, about 250 ms TLS handshake from Europe to the default US host), events from short commands like --help are usually dropped; longer commands flush in the background while they run.

Self-host PostHog or use a different project by setting POSTHOG_API_KEY and POSTHOG_HOST.

Contributing

Contributions welcome. See the open issues for things to work on, and read CONTRIBUTING.md before opening a pull request.

releases.name: Archon CLI v0.13.2
releases.body:
Upgrading from 0.13.0 with providers installed works in one command again.

### Fixed

- `archon provider add` and `archon plugin update` now replace a maintained provider installed by 0.13.0, whose receipt declares the older plugin protocol, including several providers in one command. On 0.13.1 they refused, saying the executable "may belong to a plugin whose receipt cannot be read", so the documented upgrade step failed and workflows that used that provider stopped loading. A file with an unreadable receipt or a different plugin ID is still refused, and the existing repair for a provider's own malformed receipt is unchanged. (#5287)
- `archon isolation cleanup` help and the CLI reference describe the container threshold as age since the environment was created, which is what cleanup uses. (#5283)
- The source-install guide points to the Bun version the repository pins instead of `>= 1.0.0`. (#5275)

**macOS / Linux**
```bash
curl -fsSL https://archon.diy/install | bash
```

**Windows (PowerShell)**
```powershell
irm https://archon.diy/install.ps1 | iex
```

**Homebrew (macOS / Linux)**
```bash
brew install coleam00/archon/archon

> **Upgrading from 0.13.0 with providers installed:** use [v0.13.2](https://github.com/coleam00/Archon/releases/tag/v0.13.2). In 0.13.1, `archon provider add` refused to replace providers installed by 0.13.0 (#5272). 0.13.2 fixes it, and `archon provider add claude codex pi` works in one step.

### Breaking

- The provider plugin protocol is now 3. After upgrading, run `archon provider add` again for each provider you use. Third-party provider plugins must rebuild against protocol 3. A provider installed by 0.13.0 is reported as unavailable, naming its protocol, this Archon's protocol and the command that fixes it, instead of failing workflow discovery with `Invalid input`. (#5252, #5270)

releases.body:
Slack runs only as a plugin. Declared MCP servers and misplaced node keys fail before any tokens are spent. Completed runs clean up their own worktrees and scratch space. The SDLC merge queue merges clean PRs at once, and queue answers continue without waiting for the next pass.

### Breaking

- The server no longer contains a Slack adapter; Slack runs only as the `chat-slack` plugin. Docker images ship a verified release and install it offline on startup when `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` is set, including on existing volumes, and boot logs explain what was installed; valid installed versions are kept. Removing the plugin while tokens are still set reinstalls it on restart, so remove the tokens from every env source too to keep Slack off. Outside Docker, run `archon plugin add coleam00/Archon/plugins/chat-slack` and restart. releases.name: Archon CLI v0.12.1
releases.body:
Release binaries no longer hand a target repository's `.env` to providers.

### Security

- Release binaries, including the Claude, Codex and Pi provider plugins and the forge-github and chat-slack plugins, no longer load `.env` or `bunfig.toml` from their working directory. In v0.12.0 a provider started in a target repository loaded that repository's `.env` and undid Archon's strip of it, so a project's `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` could reach Claude and override your subscription. Source installs were not affected. If you ran v0.12.0 in a repository whose `.env` holds provider keys, upgrade, then run `archon provider add` again for each provider you use. (#4426, #4427)


## Installation

### Quick Install (Recommended)

**macOS / Linux**
```bash
curl -fsSL https://archon.diy/install | bash
```

**Windows (PowerShell)**
```powershell
irm https://archon.diy/install.ps1 | iex
```

**Homebrew (macOS / Linux)**
```bash
brew install coleam00/archon/archon
```

**Docker**
```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/workspace" ghcr.io/coleam00/archon:latest workflow list
```

### Manual Installation

curl -fsSL https://github.com/coleam00/Archon/releases/latest/download/a

releases.name: Archon CLI v0.12.0
releases.body:
Providers become separate installs for release binaries. The SDLC pack gains intake, build and merge queues, a discoveries drain and attention pauses. Runs wait out usage and rate limits. Workflows can run without a database, keep durable state, and answer through one attention queue.

**Upgrading a release binary (quick installer, Homebrew, GitHub asset): add your providers.** Release binaries no longer include Claude, Codex or Pi. After upgrading, run:

```bash
archon provider add claude codex pi   # only the ones you use
```

or `archon setup`, which asks. Until you do, a workflow or chat message that needs a provider fails before it starts and prints this command, and `archon doctor` fails with the same command. aiSummary.oneLiner: An open-source harness builder designed to make AI coding workflows deterministic and repeatable.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: Archon addresses the inherent unpredictability of LLM-based coding tools by providing a framework to build deterministic execution harnesses. It allows developers to define strict boundaries, state transitions, and validation steps that an AI agent must adhere to during code generation. By wrapping the AI's execution in a controlled harness, it ensures that outputs meet specific architectural standards and pass automated tests before being presented to the user. The system intercepts hallucinations or infinite loops, forcing the agent to self-correct based on explicit error feedback. This transforms stochastic AI code generation into a reliable, pipeline-ready process.
keyFeatures: Deterministic Workflows: Enforces strict state machines that dictate exactly how an AI agent progresses through a coding task.
Automated Validation: Integrates directly with testing frameworks to automatically reject and iterate on failing AI-generated code.
State Rollbacks: Automatically reverts the codebase to a clean state if the agent's proposed changes cause compilation or logic errors.
Audit Logging: Records the complete prompt chain and execution path to ensure total transparency in how the AI reached its solution.
Framework Agnostic: Designed to wrap around various underlying LLMs and coding agents without being locked into a specific provider.

useCases.title: Automated Test Generation
useCases.description: QA teams use Archon to ensure AI-generated test suites compile successfully and achieve required coverage metrics before committing.

useCases.title: Safe Refactoring
useCases.description: Engineers deploy the harness to allow AI agents to refactor legacy code, relying on the automated rollback if integration tests fail.

useCases.title: Pipeline Integration
useCases.description: DevOps engineers integrate AI code generation directly into CI/CD pipelines, confident that the harness will enforce strict quality gates.

useCases.title: Agent Benchmarking
useCases.description: AI researchers utilize the deterministic environment to accurately measure and compare the coding proficiency of different foundation models.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: Software engineers, DevOps professionals, and AI researchers who require reliability and strict control over AI-generated code. Familiarity with testing frameworks and pipeline automation is necessary.
